string-array.name: municipalities_array
string-array.item: Beijing is the capital of China and one of the country’s four centrally administered municipalities. It is the national political and cultural centre and has been an important capital for several dynasties. The city combines historic landmarks, such as the Forbidden City, the Temple of Heaven, hutong neighbourhoods and sections of the Great Wall, with modern business, technology and education districts. Beijing’s Central Axis reflects more than 750 years of urban planning and continues to shape the city’s layout. Today, Beijing is also a major centre for government, universities, research, innovation and international exchanges.

Shanghai is a centrally administered municipality on China’s eastern coast, near the mouth of the Yangtze River. It developed from an important trading port into one of China’s most international cities. The Bund and the former concession areas show layers of modern history, while Pudong’s skyline represents rapid economic growth. Shanghai is a major centre for finance, trade, shipping, technology, culture and consumer services. Its official development plans continue to strengthen its position as an international financial centre. With busy commercial streets, museums, universities and global businesses, Shanghai combines Chinese traditions with a strongly international urban character.

Chongqing is a centrally administered municipality in Southwest China, located where the Yangtze and Jialing rivers meet. Its mountainous landscape has earned it the name “Mountain City”, while fog, steep streets and river views are familiar features. Chongqing has a long history and is closely associated with Bayu culture. Today it is an important inland centre for manufacturing, transport, trade and economic development. Visitors know the city for its night scenery, hotpot, river crossings, and attractions such as the Dazu Rock Carvings and nearby karst landscapes. Chongqing combines a large urban economy with distinctive natural scenery.

Tianjin is a centrally administered municipality in northern China, close to Beijing and facing the Bohai Sea. Its name means “the Emperor’s Port” and dates from the Ming dynasty. Historically, the city grew as a river port, military stronghold and gateway to Beijing. Tianjin later became an important centre for foreign trade and modern industry, leaving a mixture of Chinese and European-style architecture. Today, it remains a major coastal, industrial and commercial city with strengths in port services, manufacturing, finance and technology. Its riverside areas, historic streets and cultural districts reflect both traditional and international influences.
